units: Adaptive Permeability: A Dynamical Theory of System Survival Under Changing Environments.
The repository presents Adaptive Permeability as a dynamical theory of system survival under changing environments.
Complex systems are described as failing when self-revision cannot keep pace with changing constraints, rather than because goal achievement is impossible.
Adaptive survival is proposed to be governed by the relationship between effective revision capacity and environmental-change velocity.
A system is proposed to survive when its rate of generating reality-coupled adaptive capacity exceeds the rate at which reality changes required constraints.
C_rev,t is revision capacity: ability to modify internal structure, processes, or policies.
kappa_t is the permeability coefficient: degree to which external reality successfully influences internal revision.
A system may change rapidly while remaining disconnected from the environment that determines whether those changes are useful.
dot(K_eff,t) is the rate of generating effective adaptive capacity.
v_req,t = dot(X*_t) is the velocity of changing environmental requirements.
The invariant is stated to define three adaptive regimes.
Under adaptive surplus, reality-coupled capacity increases faster than environmental constraints change.
Adaptive surplus is stated to yield increased resilience.
Under critical tracking, the system exactly matches environmental velocity.
Critical tracking is stated to permit survival without adaptive margin.
Under adaptive debt, environmental change exceeds the system's ability to restructure.
A system in adaptive debt may continue functioning temporarily through stored reserves.
Adaptive debt is stated to accumulate structural debt.
Current performance is described as a lagging indicator.
A system can perform well while losing its ability to adapt.
tau_a is adaptation latency: time required to recover after an environmental perturbation.
Positive adaptation-velocity interpretation uses d tau_a/dt < 0.
Decreasing adaptation latency is interpreted as becoming faster at recovering from future shocks.
Negative adaptation-velocity interpretation uses d tau_a/dt > 0.
Increasing adaptation latency is interpreted as accumulating structural friction.
A_t = integral_0^t exp[-lambda(t-tau)] Psi_tau d tau.
Past adaptations lose value when they no longer match current reality.
A resilient system is stated to require continuous generation of new adaptive capital.
Adaptive capacity is stated not to grow without limit.
B_adapt represents available computational, energetic, organizational, or biological resources.
Environmental velocity exceeds the adaptive production limit when v_req > dot(K_eff).
When v_req > dot(K_eff), the system is stated to inevitably enter Lambda < 1.
The Adaptive Permeability Experiment (APE) is specified to test whether the invariant predicts future resilience.
APE specifies three agents operating under identical resource constraints.
Agent A is a standard learner that learns current tasks but cannot restructure its adaptation mechanism.
Agent B is a permeability adapter with an adaptive substrate capable of discovering improved revision pathways.
Agent C is a fake adapter producing high internal change velocity but low environmental coupling.
Agent C prediction: v_rev increases while kappa decreases.
Agent C is predicted to have Psi_C < 0.
All agents may initially achieve similar performance: R_A approximately R_B approximately R_C.
Environmental acceleration alpha is defined as d v_req/dt.
The future-recovery prediction is evaluated under increasing environmental acceleration.
Predicted future recovery-latency ordering: tau_future,B < tau_future,A < tau_future,C.
The theory is specified as falsified if positive adaptation velocity does not predict improved recovery under unseen future shocks.
Intelligence is defined not as solving today's environment but as becoming structurally harder to defeat by tomorrow's environment.
Adaptive systems are defined by reality-coupled capacity generated while changing, rather than by amount of change alone.
The permeability coefficient is described as a degree of external influence, but no numerical range, scale, or estimator is specified.
Revision capacity C_rev has a verbal definition but no operational measurement procedure or units.
X*_t appears only through dot(X*_t) as changing environmental requirements; its state space, metric, and units are not specified.
The source gives threshold comparisons Lambda to 1 but does not specify normalization or dimensional commensurability between dot(K_eff) and v_req.
K_eff is defined as kappa*C_rev, but source-local dynamics/estimators for kappa and C_rev sufficient to measure dot(K_eff) are not specified.
Psi is called an empirical observable but its kappa factor has no source-local measurement protocol.
Adaptation latency tau_a lacks a source-local perturbation, recovery-threshold, aggregation, or sampling protocol.
The obsolescence parameter lambda has no source-local units, estimator, or selection rule.
B_adapt names heterogeneous computational, energetic, organizational, or biological resources without a common scale or measurement procedure.
APE requires identical resource constraints but does not operationalize equivalence across the agents beyond N_params and C_compute being constant.
APE specifies agent roles but no executable architecture, learning rule, restructuring mechanism, or parameterization.
v_rev is used for Agent C internal change velocity but is not otherwise defined or operationalized.
R_A, R_B, and R_C denote initial performance without a source-local definition or measurement procedure for R.
tau_future,A/B/C are used in the predicted ordering without a source-local definition distinct from or linked explicitly to tau_a.
Increasing environmental acceleration is named as the stress condition, but its schedule, range, perturbation family, and unseen-shock distribution are unspecified.
